You use verbs with a fixed preposition (sich kümmern um, warten auf, denken an, sich freuen auf/über) and replace things with darum, darauf, daran, and in questions with worum, worauf, woran.
the ward management, the ward sister
What are you waiting for? – The doctor.

Learn verbs with a fixed preposition together with the preposition and the case (warten auf + A).
Replace a thing or an idea with da(r)- + preposition: Ich warte darauf.
Ask about things with wo(r)- + preposition: Worauf wartest du?
Use preposition + pronoun for people: Ich warte auf ihn. / Auf wen wartest du?
Use darauf / daran as an “announcement” for a clause: Ich freue mich darauf, dass du kommst.
It's February 2033. Grete Hoffmann, 96, is in hospital with pneumonia, on Mara's ward of all places. Friedrich has been sitting by her bed for three days. Mara comes for the evening round.
Good evening, Mrs Hoffmann. How are you feeling today? Your temperature has gone down, I saw.
Mara, child. I'm fine. But I'm worried about Friedrich. He's been sitting on this chair for three days. He doesn't eat anything. He doesn't sleep.
I'm waiting for you. What else should I wait for? I waited sixty-nine years for you. Another three days are nothing.
Mr Mertens, I'm looking after Mrs Hoffmann. It's my ward. You can rely on that. But you must go home and sleep.
Friedrich. I'm asking you for something. Just one thing.
Go home. Sleep. And tomorrow bring me the sheet music. The Brahms sonata. I want to think about it while I'm lying here. About the evening in your flat, 2030. Do you remember it?
Of course I remember it. I think about it every day.
When you've recovered, Mrs Hoffmann, you'll play it again. I'm already looking forward to it.
Did you hear, Friedrich? The nurse said so. So go. I'll wait for you here. I promise.
“sich Sorgen machen um” = to worry about
“sich freuen auf” = to look forward to (future)
“da-ROWF / vo-ROWF”: stress on the second syllable.
Many German verbs have a fixed preposition. The preposition doesn't always match the one you'd use in English, so learn the verb together with it:
to be pleased about (what has been / is)
“sich freuen auf” = about something that's coming (Ich freue mich auf den Urlaub). “sich freuen über” = about something you've already got (Ich freue mich über das Geschenk).
2. da(r)- + preposition: for things and ideas
When you refer back to a THING or an IDEA, you don't say “auf es”, but da- + preposition (dar- before a vowel):
Kümmerst du dich um das Essen?
Hast du Angst vor der Prüfung?
dar- appears before vowels: darauf, daran, darum, darüber. Otherwise: dafür, davon, damit, davor.
For PEOPLE you keep the preposition and add the personal pronoun:
Common mistake: “Ich warte darauf” for a person ✗. For people: “auf ihn / auf sie”.
4. da(r)- as an announcement for a clause
The da(r)- word can “announce” a dass clause or an infinitive with zu:
I'm thinking of bringing the sheet music tomorrow.
It depends on how she feels tomorrow.
What are you thinking about? – The holiday.
Who are you thinking about? – My mum.
I'm looking forward to the holidays.

Grete Hoffmann had come into hospital on a Sunday morning at the beginning of February, with a high temperature and a cough that sounded so deep that the carer at the care home had called the emergency doctor straight away. Pneumonia. At ninety-six, the emergency doctor had told Friedrich in the ambulance, that is very dangerous. Friedrich hadn't answered. He had just held Grete's hand the whole way, and then at the hospital he had sunk onto a chair next to her bed and hadn't got up again.

It was chance that she ended up on Ward 4. Or maybe not. Since January Mara had been the new ward sister, the youngest the hospital had ever had. Six years after she had come from Sibiu to Berlin as a young nurse, with a suitcase, a dictionary and A2 German, she was now responsible for thirty-two beds, eighteen nursing staff and a shift rota that blew up again every month. When on Monday morning she read the list of new admissions and saw the name “Hoffmann, Margarete, born 1936”, she put down her coffee and ran down the corridor.

She found Grete in room 412, by the window, very small and very white among the white pillows, with an oxygen tube in her nose. Friedrich sat next to her holding her hand. He looked up when Mara came in and for a moment didn't recognise her in her blue uniform. Then he just said: “Mara. Thank God.” Mara checked the readings on the monitor, read the chart, had a quick word with the night nurse. Then she sat down on the edge of the bed and put her hand on Grete's forehead. “You're in good hands, Mrs Hoffmann,” she said quietly, even though Grete was asleep. “I'll see to that personally.”

The first three days were hard. Grete was given oxygen and antibiotics and slept almost all the time. Friedrich sat next to her, at ninety-eight, in his grey suit, which he refused to take off, and waited. He waited for the ward round, for the test results, for every word from Dr Aydın, the consultant, who came every morning at eight and said the same thing every morning: “We have to wait and see.” Friedrich nodded every time. Waiting was something he knew how to do. Here he had sixty-nine years of experience.

Mara took care of everything. She made sure Friedrich got a more comfortable chair, then a recliner, then a bed in the room next door, which he didn't use. She brought him soup from the canteen, which he didn't eat, and coffee, which he drank. She rang Ludwig, and Ludwig came every afternoon, by tram, with the new app that told him which tram was coming step-free. He sat down next to Friedrich, two old men side by side, and they talked about everything: about trams, about the Wall, about Hertha BSC, about the weather. There was only one thing they didn't talk about. The thing they were both afraid of.

Once, on the third afternoon, when Grete was asleep and it was already getting dark outside, Friedrich suddenly said, without looking at Ludwig: “Do you know what I think about all the time? The thirteenth of August 1961. I was standing on Bernauer Straße watching them string up the barbed wire. I knew she was on the other side. I thought: it'll last a few weeks. Then I'll see her again.” He was silent for a long time. “It lasted sixty-nine years. And now I'm afraid of losing her again after three years.” Ludwig put his hand on his arm and said nothing. There was nothing to say to that.

On the fourth evening the fever went down. Grete opened her eyes, looked around, saw Friedrich on his chair, unshaven, with red eyes, in his crumpled suit, and said in a hoarse voice: “You look terrible.” Friedrich laughed, for the first time in four days, then cried, then laughed again. And then Mara came on her evening round and heard Grete sending him home, and understood why these two people had waited sixty-nine years for each other.

Dr Aydın, who was still on duty that evening, dropped in briefly, looked at the readings, listened to Grete with his stethoscope and smiled for the first time. “Mrs Hoffmann,” he said, “I have to admit: I was very worried about you. But your lungs are stronger than my statistics.” Grete looked at him over the top of her glasses, which Friedrich had put on for her. “Young man,” she said, “I've survived a war, a Wall and a husband who didn't deserve me. I'll manage a case of pneumonia too.” Dr Aydın laughed so loudly that the nurses in the corridor stopped.

Friedrich went home, for the first time in four days. Ludwig went with him, by tram, to the door of the care home, and waited until the light went on upstairs in his room, and half an hour later went off. Then he went home. And the next morning at seven, an hour before visiting time, Friedrich was standing outside Ward 4 again, shaved, in a clean shirt, with a folder under his arm. Inside it was the sheet music of the Brahms sonata, yellowed, with Grete's pencil notes from 1958, and next to it, in a plastic sleeve, a photo of her at the piano, at twenty.
Mara, sit with me a moment. I have to ask you something. And you have to promise me you won't say no.
Mrs Hoffmann, I don't promise anything before I know what it's about. I learnt that from Ludwig.

Clever girl. Well then: I won't live for ever. I'm ninety-six. When I'm gone, look after Friedrich. Not as a nurse. As a friend. He has nobody except me and Sophie, and Sophie lives in Lübeck. He won't say so, he never says anything. But he'll need you. Do you promise me?

Mara looked at the old woman who, six years ago, on the fourth floor on Kastanienallee, had offered her her first coffee, in a flat full of books with a black 1958 Steinway by the window. Who had taught her German, not from books, but with stories. Who had told her how she had played the piano during the war, in the cellar, so that the children wouldn't be afraid of the bombs. Mara thought about how often this woman had looked after others. And she said: “Yes. I promise. But not so soon, Mrs Hoffmann. I insist on that.”

That evening Mara didn't get home until ten, to the flat on the fourth floor where Grete used to live. Jakob was waiting for her with soup that he had heated up twice. She sat down with her plate by the living-room window, exactly where Grete's Steinway had stood six years ago, and told him everything. Jakob listened without interrupting. Then he said: “You promised her something that can't really be promised.” “I know,” said Mara. “But sometimes that's exactly what you have to do. Otherwise the other person can't sleep in peace.” Jakob took her hand and looked at her for a long time, as if he wanted to say something. But then he didn't, and Mara didn't notice.

Grete laughed, a hoarse, weak laugh that immediately turned into a cough. Then she took the sheet music Friedrich had brought and laid it on the duvet, and her long, thin fingers moved over the paper, bar by bar, as if she were playing. Friedrich sat beside her and hummed the melody quietly. And Mara, who actually had twelve other patients, a shift rota that was blowing up and a meeting with the consultant in ten minutes, stayed in the doorway and listened until the sonata was over.

Twelve days later Grete was discharged. Ludwig and Friedrich picked her up in a taxi, because Friedrich insisted that she shouldn't go by tram, not even step-free. At the care home the other residents were waiting in the common room, with a cake and a sign painted by Elif: “Welcome back, Mrs Hoffmann!” Grete sat down at the piano, even though Dr Aydın had forbidden it, and played three bars. Then she put her hands in her lap and said: “That's enough for today. I'll play the rest on my birthday.” And everyone in the room knew she meant it.

In the evening Mara wrote in her little notebook, in which for six years she had noted a new German word every day, one single word. It wasn't a new word. She had known it since her first month in Berlin. But only now, she thought, did she understand what it really means: “to take care”.
